title: Ready state semantics + API notes (control plane/routing) — Dedicated provisioning
content:
Context
- We historically had a fairly loose “pool registration” model: data plane brings up a cluster, calls register/update, control plane marks it as available, routing starts sending traffic (sometimes w/ manual checks).
- Provision-to-ready automation introduces staged lifecycle + gates. Control plane needs to represent “infra exists but not safe to route” and make that default.
- Goal of these notes: agree on (1) semantics of Ready vs other states, (2) API surface for automation + consumers, (3) backward compatibility for existing registration clients.

Terminology (proposed)
- Pool: the unit routing allocates capacity from (Dedicated customer pool, internal staging pool, etc.)
- Provisioning run: a single execution of the pipeline (may be retried, may be paused/resumed).
- Stage: named segment within a run (Provisioning, Imaging, Bootstrapping, Validating, PerfCanary).

High-level principle
- “Ready” MUST be the only state that makes a pool eligible for routing (except any explicit emergency override, which should be very loud + audited).
- “Validating” is NOT eligible. Routing treating Validating as usable is the main footgun we want to eliminate.

Ready semantics (what “Ready” means)
A pool may be marked Ready only if ALL are true:
1) Control plane has a successful provisioning run for the current pool generation (see generation notes below).
2) Infrastructure resources exist and are reachable from required control planes (k8s API reachable from provisioner; nodes registered; expected labels/taints present).
3) Required base image version has been applied (or equivalent attestation if we support multiple images).
4) Bootstrap completed (runtime chart installed/pinned versions, required CRDs/configs applied, secrets wiring complete).
5) Readiness gates passed:
   - Networking: DNS resolution, TLS handshake to required endpoints, egress allowlists (as applicable)
   - GPU health checks: ECC, driver match, NVML health, burn-in smoke (lightweight)
   - Runtime smoke tests: model load + small inference request path works
6) Perf-canary readiness suite passed within thresholds (p50 latency and throughput sanity; not aiming for full benchmark).
7) Pool metadata for routing is present and consistent (SKU, region, capacity numbers, compatible model families, etc.).

Non-obvious edge: “Ready” is a statement about the pool being safe to receive traffic, not a guarantee that we can hit customer SLO on all models. The perf-canary thresholds should be “sanity bounds”, not product SLA bounds.

State model
We need two related but distinct concepts:
A) Pool lifecycle state (longer-lived; what routing consumes)
B) Provisioning run state (per execution; what operators debug)

A) Pool lifecycle state (field name suggestion: lifecycle_state)
- Requested: pool exists in control plane but no infra yet / automation not started.
- Provisioning: infra being created/expanded.
- Imaging: nodes being imaged / base image verified.
- Bootstrapping: cluster/bootstrap components being installed.
- Validating: readiness gates running.
- Ready: passed validation and safe for routing.
- Failed: run failed and requires intervention OR an explicit retry.
- Paused: intentionally paused by operator/admin.

Notes:
- lifecycle_state should be derivable from “latest run state”, but we still want it persisted for consumers.
- We should NOT allow external callers to set lifecycle_state directly (except admin break-glass).

B) Provisioning run state
- Similar stage list above + timestamps; supports retries.
- A run is identified by run_id and has:
  - started_at, finished_at
  - current_stage
  - stage_attempt counters
  - last_error_code / last_error_message (operator-facing)
  - initiated_by (service identity / user)
  - correlation_id for logs/metrics

Generation / drift considerations
- We need a way to say “Ready for which config?”. Proposed: pool has config_generation integer (or hash of desired config) and the latest successful run records that generation.
- lifecycle_state=Ready means: latest_successful_run.config_generation == pool.desired_config_generation AND drift_check = clean.
- If desired config changes (new helm values, new runtime pin, scaling), desired_config_generation bumps and pool should move out of Ready until new run succeeds (or explicitly decide some changes are “non-disruptive”).

API shape (proposed)
We should support three “classes” of API calls:
1) Existing registration clients (back-compat)
2) Provisioner orchestration (new)
3) Routing consumption (new/adjusted)

1) Existing pool registration API (backward compatibility)
Assumption: there are existing data plane agents calling something like:
- POST /v1/pools/register (or update)
- PATCH /v1/pools/{pool_id}

Back-compat strategy:
- Keep accepting existing register/update payloads.
- Map legacy “registered” to a safe default state:
  - If automation is enabled for the pool/environment: registration updates metadata only, lifecycle_state remains Requested/Provisioning/etc. (i.e., registration does not imply Ready).
  - If automation is disabled (feature flag off): allow legacy behavior but still run minimal readiness checks if available; in this mode lifecycle_state may go to Ready on register (to avoid breaking old flows). This is a transitional stance.

Concrete proposal:
- Add new fields to pool resource in a way that old clients can ignore:
  - lifecycle_state (string enum)
  - ready_at (timestamp, optional)
  - latest_provisioning_run_id (string)
  - desired_config_generation (string/int)
  - applied_config_generation (string/int)
  - routing_eligibility (computed string/bool; see routing section)
- Do NOT change meaning of existing “status” field if external systems depend on it. If status exists, keep it as “Active/Inactive/Deleted” (or whatever it is today) and treat lifecycle_state as orthogonal.

2) Provisioner orchestration API (new)
Endpoints (names illustrative; exact path can change, but we need these capabilities):
- POST /v1/pools/{pool_id}/provisioning-runs
  - Starts a new run.
  - Request:
    - idempotency_key (required; stable for same intent)
    - requested_stages (optional; default full pipeline)
    - reason (string)
    - dry_run (bool; optional)
  - Response:
    - run_id
    - lifecycle_state (after transition)

- GET /v1/pools/{pool_id}/provisioning-runs/{run_id}
  - Returns run details, stage timings, failure reason, links/correlation IDs.

- POST /v1/pools/{pool_id}/provisioning-runs/{run_id}:pause
- POST /v1/pools/{pool_id}/provisioning-runs/{run_id}:resume
  - Admin-only (or limited operator role). Must emit audit log entries.

- POST /v1/pools/{pool_id}/provisioning-runs/{run_id}:rerun
  - Allows re-running validation only, or imaging+bootstrap, etc.
  - Must be safe and idempotent (or require explicit “force” parameter).

- PATCH /v1/pools/{pool_id}
  - For desired config updates, bump desired_config_generation.
  - Important: updates should NOT auto-mark Ready; they should enqueue a run.

AuthZ considerations
- Provisioning operations should be restricted:
  - provisioner service identity
  - fleet operators (limited admin)
- Routing service should have read-only access to routing_eligibility and pool metadata.

3) Routing consumption
Routing should consume a single “is this eligible?” bit/field to minimize logic duplication.
- Proposed field: routing_eligibility
  - Eligible iff lifecycle_state == Ready AND not paused AND not in cooldown/quarantine AND no active incident override.
- Routing should NOT interpret stage state; it should treat non-Ready as ineligible.

Additionally, routing should be able to query pools by eligibility:
- GET /v1/pools?customer_id=…&region=…&routing_eligibility=true

Backward compatibility notes / migration plan
Phase 0: Add fields, no behavior change
- Introduce lifecycle_state and run objects in control plane DB.
- Keep old register flow; set lifecycle_state=Ready on register ONLY when automation flag disabled.

Phase 1: Dual-write + soft enforcement
- For pools with automation enabled:
  - register updates metadata only
  - lifecycle_state driven by provisioner runs
- Routing begins to respect routing_eligibility (behind routing feature flag).

Phase 2: Hard enforcement
- Routing uses routing_eligibility universally.
- Legacy register can never mark a pool Ready (except explicit admin override / emergency mode).

Phase 3: Cleanup
- Deprecate any legacy “ready” booleans if present.
- Potentially move register endpoint to “metadata heartbeat” semantics.

Edge cases / open questions
1) Expansion vs new pool
- Do we treat expansion as a separate run that can keep existing capacity in Ready while new nodes validate?
  - Ideal: partial readiness. But it complicates eligibility (pool partially Ready).
  - MVP: pool remains Ready while adding capacity, but routing must not send traffic to unvalidated nodes.
    - That implies node-level readiness in data plane OR “shadow capacity” until nodes pass.
  - Alternate MVP: pool leaves Ready during expansion (simpler, but customer-visible impact).

2) Partial readiness model
- If we need expansion without impact, we likely need a “Ready + PendingExpansion” state or track “validated_capacity” separately.
- Recommendation for sprint MVP: keep pool eligible but don’t advertise new capacity to routing until validation passes; this requires the capacity accounting model to handle validated vs unvalidated.
- If we can’t ship validated_capacity quickly, fallback to “pool not eligible during expansion” for the pilot customer (communicated maintenance window).

3) “Validating” / “PerfCanary” failure
- On failure, do we mark lifecycle_state=Failed or stay in Validating with error?
- Suggestion: lifecycle_state=Failed with last_error_code; keep run details for debugging.

4) Operator overrides
- We will need a break-glass to set routing_eligibility=true even if lifecycle_state != Ready (e.g., perf-canary is flaky but we need capacity).
- This must be:
  - time-bounded (TTL)
  - audited
  - visible in routing and dashboards

5) Timeouts / stuck stages
- Should the control plane enforce stage deadlines? Or leave entirely to provisioner?
- Suggestion: provisioner owns retries/timeouts; control plane stores state and exposes “stuck” signal for alerting.

6) Field naming consistency
- lifecycle_state vs ready_state vs provisioning_state
- Strong preference: “lifecycle_state” for the pool; “run_state/current_stage” for runs.

Proposed minimal schema for Pool resource (non-final, just to align)
- pool_id
- customer_id
- region
- sku
- status (existing)
- lifecycle_state (new)
- routing_eligibility (new; derived)
- latest_provisioning_run_id (new)
- desired_config_generation (new)
- applied_config_generation (new)
- last_ready_at (new)
- last_error_code (new)
- last_error_message (new)

Action items (for sprint)
- [Ethan] Confirm existing pool registration clients and current semantics (what endpoints, what fields do they read/write).
- [Ravi] Wire routing consumption to routing_eligibility (or lifecycle_state==Ready) behind feature flag; do not accept Validating.
- [Vanessa + provisioner] Confirm state transitions emitted by provisioner match lifecycle_state expectations (no Ready before perf-canary completes).
- [Benji] Confirm break-glass story + audit log requirements for overrides.
- [Rafael] Confirm alerting expectations for “pool stuck not Ready” and what constitutes paging.

Notes from discussion (snippets)
- Mina: “Routing should be dumb: it gets a list of eligible pools. It shouldn’t infer semantics from intermediate states.”
- Ravi: “We should treat Ready as a contract. Anything else should be ineligible by default.”
- Vikram: “Legacy registration is used by older clusters; keep endpoint, but don’t let it flip to Ready when automation is on.”
- Rafael: “If we allow emergency overrides, it has to show up in dashboards; otherwise we’ll lose track of why a pool is serving.”
